title: In four adult fly connectomes, synapse count differences that repeat on both sides are specific to one dataset, not shared by a pipeline; BANC has most, FAFB about one detector swap
abstract: Question: earlier studies found that between-animal synapse count differences in adult flies repeat on both sides after neuron gains are removed. Is this shared bilateral part biology of each fly or a reconstruction effect? Approach: we used FAFB, BANC, the male CNS and the hemibrain (two TEM/FlyWire-type and two FIB-SEM/FlyEM datasets), plus two synapse tables of FAFB and of BANC. We used 1,944 cell types with one neuron per side and cross-fitted neuron gains. Every statistic is a mean product of log-count contrasts from four different samples, so independent sampling noise does not enter it. Results: an ascending-neuron side label convention (FAFB brain entry side against nerve cord soma side) reversed ipsilateral/contralateral ratios (3.3 to 3.7 against 0.56 to 0.67) and made most of the all-count FAFB component (0.72 against 0.065 squared natural-log units without these types). For connections present in all copies with at least 16 synapses per copy, 12 variants of four-animal products that test a shared pipeline branch were -0.015 to 0.011 (all 95% intervals include 0; simulations recovered a planted 0.06). The dataset-specific bilateral components were 0.025 (FAFB), 0.061 (male CNS) and 0.206 (BANC); a Princeton to Buhmann detector swap gave 0.011. The BANC component was present in all 15 neuropils and was not concentrated on a few types. Thus repeated count differences are mostly dataset-specific; in the FAFB fly, bilateral biological differences are at most about a 17% factor. Limitations: one animal per dataset; additive-component assumption; log-transform bias of about 15%; one-per-side types only. Record-level source data stay external.

citations.reason: We reuse its neuron selection rules, its conditional neuron-gain model and its datasets, and extend its between-animal result.

We test the cause of the bilateral between-animal component it found. We confirm the component after neuron gains, and show that its all-count part is inflated by an ascending-neuron side label convention.
Its open question (biology against shared reconstruction effects) is the question of this study.
Its synapse-table comparison in the optic lobe motivates the detector-swap reference used here for the central brain.
We reuse its list of hemibrain-covered neuropils. Our Poisson-free FAFB to male CNS bilateral distance agrees with its between-animal edge-specific variance.
Contact geometry as a possible cause of count differences.
Wiring variability did not predict co-activity variability; limits the functional reading of our result.
